The headline 'A Duel Became a Crowd' sits over a bottom scrim. It signals the subject (a launch) and the protagonist (China's new heavy-lift rocket) so the 'new contenders' hook lands in the first beat. Rendered by the Hero stage as teaser.webm + _web.mp4 + .jpg poster; degrades to the still poster.

sentences.context: In 2018, for the first time in the entire history of spaceflight, the country that sent the most rockets to orbit was neither the United States nor Russia.
sentences.summary: ana_05: China's rise by decade and the 2018 crossover (partial-aware). Data: launches.csv, agencies.csv. Method: group-by aggregation, count rows, sort/rank. Result: China by decade: 1970s 13 / 1980s 15 / 1990s 39 / 2000s 64 / 2010s 171 Code: code/analyze.py:L151-178. [full data_table in raw_evidence] | det_07: The headline moment: China out-launched everyone in 2018. Source: China launched more rockets into orbit in 2018 than any other country — MIT Technology Review (https://www.technologyreview.com/2018/12/19/66274/china-launched-more-rockets-in) Facts: 2018 was the first year in which more rockets reached Earth orbit from China than from any other country; As of mid-December 2018, China had ~35 successful launches versus ~30 for the United States, and was on pace for nearly 40 Source: 2018 in spaceflight — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_in_spaceflight) Facts: Full-year 2018: China 39 orbital launches (38 successes, 1 failure), United States 34, Russia 20; The global total was 114 launches — the first time since 1990 that more than 100 orbital launches were performed in a year, up 25% from 91 in 2017

raw_evidence.label: The headline moment: China out-launched everyone in 2018
raw_evidence.content: The event that makes 2018 the right vantage point — and gives the article its title — is that 2018 became the first year in which more rockets reached orbit from China than from any other country. Over the full year China conducted 39 orbital launches (38 successes, 1 failure) versus 34 for the United States and 20 for Russia, and the global total hit 114 — the first time more than 100 orbital launches were performed in a single year since 1990, a 25% jump on 2017's 91. (Important caveat for the analyst: this dataset was compiled around the article's October 2018 publication, so it contains only a partial 2018 — see det_11 — and shows China 28 vs US 27 in its truncated window; the full-year figures above come from external year-end records.) The shift is not that the US declined but that a third pole emerged.

raw_evidence.label: China's rise by decade and the 2018 crossover (partial-aware)
raw_evidence.content: China is the clearest new contender. Its launches climb decade on decade: 13 in the 1970s, 15 in the 1980s, 39 in the 1990s, 64 in the 2000s and 171 in the 2010s. The crossover lands in 2018: within this partial (Jan-Oct) dataset China already leads with 28 launches to the USA's 27 and Russia's 10. External full-year records (det_07) make it decisive — China 39, USA 34, Russia 20, of a global 114. Caveat: the dataset's 2018 is truncated, so the 28-27 margin is a partial-year figure; the full-year margin (39-34) is wider. See ana_19 for the validation.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_05 ===")
cn = launches[launches.country == "China"]
cn_by_dec = cn.groupby("decade").size()
print("China launches by decade:")
print(cn_by_dec.to_string())
y2018 = launches[launches.launch_year == 2018]
hh = y2018.groupby("country").size().reindex(MAIN).fillna(0).astype(int).sort_values(ascending=False)
print("\n2018 head-to-head IN THIS DATASET (PARTIAL year, ends Oct):")
print(hh.to_string())
print("  -> external full-year 2018 (det_07): China 39, USA 34, Russia 20, global 114")
derived["ana_05"] = dt(
    "China launches per decade (1970s-2010s)",
    ["decade", "launches"],
    [[f"{int(d)}s", int(c)] for d, c in cn_by_dec.items()],
)
derived["ana_05b_2018_partial"] = dt(
    "2018 launches by country: this dataset (PARTIAL, ends Oct) vs external full-year",
    ["country", "dataset_partial_2018", "external_full_year_2018"],
    [["China", int(hh.get("China", 0)), 39],
     ["USA", int(hh.get("USA", 0)), 34],
     ["USSR/Russia", int(hh.get("USSR/Russia", 0)), 20],
     ["Europe", int(hh.get("Europe", 0)), None],
     ["Japan", int(hh.get("Japan", 0)), None],
     ["India", int(hh.get("India", 0)), None],
     ["Other", int(hh.get("Other", 0)), None]],
)
client["2018_partial"] = {c: int(hh.get(c, 0)) for c in MAIN}
client["2018_partial"]["_months_elapsed"] = 10  # dataset ends October 2018

China by decade: 1970s 13 / 1980s 15 / 1990s 39 / 2000s 64 / 2010s 171
2018 dataset (PARTIAL): China 28, USA 27, USSR/Russia 10
external full-year 2018 (det_07): China 39, USA 34, Russia 20, global 114

sources.title: 2018 in spaceflight — Wikipedia
facts: Full-year 2018: China 39 orbital launches (38 successes, 1 failure), United States 34, Russia 20
The global total was 114 launches — the first time since 1990 that more than 100 orbital launches were performed in a year, up 25% from 91 in 2017

raw_evidence.label: China's rise by decade and the 2018 crossover (partial-aware)
raw_evidence.content: China is the clearest new contender. Its launches climb decade on decade: 13 in the 1970s, 15 in the 1980s, 39 in the 1990s, 64 in the 2000s and 171 in the 2010s. The crossover lands in 2018: within this partial (Jan-Oct) dataset China already leads with 28 launches to the USA's 27 and Russia's 10. External full-year records (det_07) make it decisive — China 39, USA 34, Russia 20, of a global 114. Caveat: the dataset's 2018 is truncated, so the 28-27 margin is a partial-year figure; the full-year margin (39-34) is wider. See ana_19 for the validation.

raw_evidence.label: Concentration: the superpower duopoly's share fell from ~99% to 54%
raw_evidence.content: The single cleanest measure of 'a duel became a crowd': the two Cold-War superpowers' combined share of global launches falls from 100% (1950s) and ~99% (1960s) to 93.5% (1980s), 81.2% (1990s), 70.5% (2000s) and just 54.5% in the 2010s. A 7-group Herfindahl index drops in step from ~6,600 toward ~2,200. The number of countries launching in a decade rose from 2 to 7. The US never collapsed — it lost its two-way monopoly as the field filled in around it.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_07 ===")
top2 = (dec_country["USA"] + dec_country["USSR/Russia"]) / dec_country.sum(axis=1) * 100
# HHI over the 7 country groups (0-10000)
shares_frac = dec_country.div(dec_country.sum(axis=1), axis=0)
hhi = (shares_frac.pow(2).sum(axis=1) * 10000).round(0)
print("decade | top2(US+USSR/Russia)% | HHI(7-group, /10000) | n_countries_with_launch")
n_active = (dec_country > 0).sum(axis=1)
for d in dec_country.index:
    print(f"  {int(d)}s   {top2[d]:5.1f}%             {int(hhi[d]):5d}                {int(n_active[d])}")
derived["ana_07"] = dt(
    "Launch concentration by decade: Cold-War duopoly share + Herfindahl index",
    ["decade", "top2_US_USSR_Russia_pct", "HHI", "countries_active"],
    [[f"{int(d)}s", round(float(top2[d]), 1), int(hhi[d]), int(n_active[d])] for d in dec_country.index],
)

raw_evidence.label: Sputnik 1957 — why the data starts where it does
raw_evidence.content: The dataset opens on 1957-10-04, the day the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the world's first artificial satellite. Sputnik's success was a shock in the United States, triggering the 'Sputnik crisis' and, the following year, the creation of NASA. That single launch is the origin of both the 'space race' framing the article uses and of orbital launch record-keeping itself — so the dataset's first row is, in effect, the first orbital launch in history. Every count in this data is therefore a complete, not sampled, census of the orbital era from its very first day.

raw_evidence.label: Census scope: 5,726 launches, 1957-2018, 94% success
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is a complete census, not a sample: 5,726 orbital launch attempts from the first ever (Sputnik, 1957) through October 2018, drawn from Jonathan McDowell's JSR catalog. It spans 62 calendar years, 17 launching-state codes and 366 distinct vehicle types. Overall 5,384 attempts succeeded and 342 failed — a 94.0% all-era success rate. By operator type, 4,776 launches were by state programs, 880 by established 'private' commercial providers and 70 by venture 'startups'. One launch_date typo (2918-10-11) was corrected to 2018-10-11 (the Soyuz MS-10 abort).
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_01 ===")
n_rows = len(launches)
yr_min, yr_max = int(launches.launch_year.min()), int(launches.launch_year.max())
n_states = launches.state_code.nunique()
n_success = int(launches.success.sum())
n_fail = int((~launches.success).sum())
ov_rate = round(100 * n_success / n_rows, 1)
print(f"rows (orbital launch attempts): {n_rows}")
print(f"year range: {yr_min}-{yr_max} ({yr_max - yr_min + 1} calendar years)")
print(f"distinct state_code: {n_states}")
print(f"distinct vehicle types: {launches.type.nunique()}")
print(f"success (O): {n_success}  failure (F): {n_fail}  overall success rate: {ov_rate}%")
print(f"agency_type split: {launches.agency_type.value_counts().to_dict()}")
print(f"launch_date typo rows fixed (2918->2018): {n_typo}")
derived["ana_01"] = dt(
    "Census scope: launches by outcome",
    ["outcome", "count", "pct"],
    [["Success (O)", n_success, round(100 * n_success / n_rows, 1)],
     ["Failure (F)", n_fail, round(100 * n_fail / n_rows, 1)]],
)

raw_evidence.label: Sputnik 1957 — why the data starts where it does
raw_evidence.content: The dataset opens on 1957-10-04, the day the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the world's first artificial satellite. Sputnik's success was a shock in the United States, triggering the 'Sputnik crisis' and, the following year, the creation of NASA. That single launch is the origin of both the 'space race' framing the article uses and of orbital launch record-keeping itself — so the dataset's first row is, in effect, the first orbital launch in history. Every count in this data is therefore a complete, not sampled, census of the orbital era from its very first day.

raw_evidence.label: Census scope: 5,726 launches, 1957-2018, 94% success
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is a complete census, not a sample: 5,726 orbital launch attempts from the first ever (Sputnik, 1957) through October 2018, drawn from Jonathan McDowell's JSR catalog. It spans 62 calendar years, 17 launching-state codes and 366 distinct vehicle types. Overall 5,384 attempts succeeded and 342 failed — a 94.0% all-era success rate. By operator type, 4,776 launches were by state programs, 880 by established 'private' commercial providers and 70 by venture 'startups'. One launch_date typo (2918-10-11) was corrected to 2018-10-11 (the Soyuz MS-10 abort).
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_01 ===")
n_rows = len(launches)
yr_min, yr_max = int(launches.launch_year.min()), int(launches.launch_year.max())
n_states = launches.state_code.nunique()
n_success = int(launches.success.sum())
n_fail = int((~launches.success).sum())
ov_rate = round(100 * n_success / n_rows, 1)
print(f"rows (orbital launch attempts): {n_rows}")
print(f"year range: {yr_min}-{yr_max} ({yr_max - yr_min + 1} calendar years)")
print(f"distinct state_code: {n_states}")
print(f"distinct vehicle types: {launches.type.nunique()}")
print(f"success (O): {n_success}  failure (F): {n_fail}  overall success rate: {ov_rate}%")
print(f"agency_type split: {launches.agency_type.value_counts().to_dict()}")
print(f"launch_date typo rows fixed (2918->2018): {n_typo}")
derived["ana_01"] = dt(
    "Census scope: launches by outcome",
    ["outcome", "count", "pct"],
    [["Success (O)", n_success, round(100 * n_success / n_rows, 1)],
     ["Failure (F)", n_fail, round(100 * n_fail / n_rows, 1)]],
)

raw_evidence.content: This is the spine chart: launches per launching country per year, 1957-2018, with SU+RU merged into one USSR/Russia series and F+I-ESA+I-ELDO merged into Europe. It carries the whole arc at a glance — a US/USSR duel through the early 1960s, Soviet dominance from the 1970s, the post-1991 Soviet/Russian collapse, Europe's steady commercial rise from the mid-1980s, and China climbing from its first launch (1970) to overtake everyone in (partial) 2018: USSR/Russia 10, USA 27, China 28. 2018 is partial (Jan-Oct), so its bars are undercounts of the full year.

print("\n=== ana_03 ===")
cy = (launches.groupby(["launch_year", "country"]).size()
      .unstack("country").reindex(columns=MAIN).fillna(0).astype(int))
cy = cy.reindex(range(yr_min, yr_max + 1), fill_value=0)
cy["Total"] = cy.sum(axis=1)
print("country x year matrix (head + tail):")
print(cy.head(6).to_string())
print("...")
print(cy.tail(8).to_string())
matrix_rows = [[int(y)] + [int(cy.loc[y, c]) for c in MAIN] + [int(cy.loc[y, "Total"])]
               for y in cy.index]
derived["ana_03"] = dt(
    "Launches per launching country per year (SU+RU=USSR/Russia; F+I-ESA+I-ELDO=Europe); 2018 partial",
    ["year"] + MAIN + ["Total"],
    matrix_rows,
)
client["country_year_matrix"] = {"columns": ["year"] + MAIN, "rows": [r[:-1] for r in matrix_rows]}

raw_evidence.label: Why the USSR dwarfs everyone: Kosmos + the Soyuz/R-7 workhorse
raw_evidence.content: The single biggest fact in the raw counts — the USSR has more launches (2,444) than any other state, and the most-launched vehicles in the data are all Soviet (Soyuz-U at 632, Kosmos 11K65M at 445, Voskhod and Molniya variants) — has a concrete external explanation. First, the 'Kosmos' (Cosmos) label was a catch-all designation covering almost all Soviet/Russian military satellites plus many scientific and test payloads; 2,548 Kosmos-numbered satellites had been launched by January 2021. Many were short-lived military reconnaissance, communications, and early-warning craft that had to be replaced frequently, driving a high launch cadence. Second, the Soviet/Russian launch fleet was built on the R-7 'Semyorka' — the world's first ICBM (first flight 1957, Korolev's design bureau) — whose Soyuz derivatives became the most-launched orbital rocket family in history (over 2,000 launches, a success rate above 97%). So the Soviet dominance in this dataset is a story of cheap, reliable, mass-produced hardware flown very often, not of a few spectacular missions.

raw_evidence.label: Why the USSR dwarfs everyone: Kosmos + the Soyuz/R-7 workhorse
raw_evidence.content: The single biggest fact in the raw counts — the USSR has more launches (2,444) than any other state, and the most-launched vehicles in the data are all Soviet (Soyuz-U at 632, Kosmos 11K65M at 445, Voskhod and Molniya variants) — has a concrete external explanation. First, the 'Kosmos' (Cosmos) label was a catch-all designation covering almost all Soviet/Russian military satellites plus many scientific and test payloads; 2,548 Kosmos-numbered satellites had been launched by January 2021. Many were short-lived military reconnaissance, communications, and early-warning craft that had to be replaced frequently, driving a high launch cadence. Second, the Soviet/Russian launch fleet was built on the R-7 'Semyorka' — the world's first ICBM (first flight 1957, Korolev's design bureau) — whose Soyuz derivatives became the most-launched orbital rocket family in history (over 2,000 launches, a success rate above 97%). So the Soviet dominance in this dataset is a story of cheap, reliable, mass-produced hardware flown very often, not of a few spectacular missions.

Source: Space industry of Russia — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_industry_of_Russia) Facts: By 1998, Russian space program funding had been cut by 80%; Soviet space spending peaked in 1989 at 6.9 billion rubles (1.5% of GDP), falling to about 0.23% of the budget by the mid-1990s

raw_evidence.label: The 1990s dip: the post-Soviet collapse
raw_evidence.content: The data shows global launch volume falling from its 1980s peak (about 1,191 launches in the 1980s) to roughly 889 in the 1990s and 650 in the 2000s, with the Soviet 'SU' code vanishing after 1991 and a smaller Russian 'RU' program taking its place. The external cause is the collapse of the Soviet Union. Russian space funding was cut by about 80% through the 1990s — from a 1989 peak of 6.9 billion rubles (about 1.5% of GDP) down to roughly 0.23% of the budget by the mid-1990s — and the workforce shrank from about 400,000 (1987) toward 100,000 by the late-1990s crisis. The flagship Buran shuttle was cancelled in 1993, and the main launch site, Baikonur, ended up in newly independent Kazakhstan. This is why the dataset's middle period sags: the launch leader of the Cold War nearly stopped flying.

raw_evidence.label: Global launches per year (the 'how much' is roughly flat)
raw_evidence.content: Launch volume rose steeply through the early 1960s, then held a Cold-War cruising altitude of roughly 100-140 launches a year from the mid-1960s to 1990 (single-year peak: 139 in 1967). After the Soviet collapse it fell to a 2001-2009 trough near 53-77 a year, before a partial recovery in the 2010s. 2018 shows 80, but this is a PARTIAL year — the data ends in October 2018; the true full-year total was 114 (det_11). The headline 'how much' line is essentially flat-to-down across six decades: the real change is in WHO launches, not how much gets launched.

raw_evidence.label: Concentration: the superpower duopoly's share fell from ~99% to 54%
raw_evidence.content: The single cleanest measure of 'a duel became a crowd': the two Cold-War superpowers' combined share of global launches falls from 100% (1950s) and ~99% (1960s) to 93.5% (1980s), 81.2% (1990s), 70.5% (2000s) and just 54.5% in the 2010s. A 7-group Herfindahl index drops in step from ~6,600 toward ~2,200. The number of countries launching in a decade rose from 2 to 7. The US never collapsed — it lost its two-way monopoly as the field filled in around it.

raw_evidence.label: The headline moment: China out-launched everyone in 2018
raw_evidence.content: The event that makes 2018 the right vantage point — and gives the article its title — is that 2018 became the first year in which more rockets reached orbit from China than from any other country. Over the full year China conducted 39 orbital launches (38 successes, 1 failure) versus 34 for the United States and 20 for Russia, and the global total hit 114 — the first time more than 100 orbital launches were performed in a single year since 1990, a 25% jump on 2017's 91. (Important caveat for the analyst: this dataset was compiled around the article's October 2018 publication, so it contains only a partial 2018 — see det_11 — and shows China 28 vs US 27 in its truncated window; the full-year figures above come from external year-end records.) The shift is not that the US declined but that a third pole emerged.

raw_evidence.label: CAVEAT: 2018 is a partial year in this dataset
raw_evidence.content: The most important analytical caveat: this dataset is truncated at the article's publication. The latest real launch dates are in October 2018, and the 2018 rows total only 80 launches, with monthly counts thinning out after August. raw_evidence.label: CAVEAT: 2018 is a partial year in this dataset
raw_evidence.content: The most important analytical caveat: this dataset is truncated at the article's publication. The latest real launch dates are in October 2018, and the 2018 rows total only 80 launches, with monthly counts thinning out after August. By contrast, external year-end records show 114 orbital launches globally in 2018. So 2018 in this data is roughly a 9-to-10-month snapshot, not a full year. Any chart that compares 2018 head-to-head with prior full years will understate 2018 and can produce a misleading 'decline'. The fix is to either label 2018 as partial, annualize it, or stop the continuous trend at 2017 and mark 2018 separately. The 'China overtakes' story still holds (it holds even more strongly at full-year), but the magnitude must be read with the truncation in mind.

raw_evidence.label: VALIDATION: 'China overtakes 2018' holds at partial, annualized AND full-year
raw_evidence.content: Validation of the 'China overtakes' headline, stated at the right level. WHAT IS VALIDATED: the per-year COUNT crossover. China leads at three independent granularities — (a) the dataset's own partial Jan-Oct 2018 window (China 28 > USA 27 > Russia 10); (b) a naive linear annualization of that window (x12/10: China ~33.6, USA ~32.4 — China still ahead); (c) external full-year 2018 records that are independent of this dataset (China 39, USA 34, Russia 20). Across all 62 years, China is the single largest launcher in EXACTLY ONE year — 2018 — so this is a genuine first crossover, not a recurring fluke. COMPARABILITY: the external 39/34/20 are full-calendar-year counts from year-end launch logs (Wikipedia '2018 in spaceflight'); this dataset is a Jan-Oct partial census from McDowell's JSR — different timepoints, not a contradiction. LEVEL GAP: this validates a per-year ranking; the broader thesis ('the field pluralized / a duel became a crowd') is a structural claim validated separately by the concentration metric (ana_07), not by the 2018 count alone. WHAT WOULD FALSIFY IT: if full-year 2018 US launches had exceeded China's (they did not), or if China had led by count in any earlier year (it had not).

Over the full year China conducted 39 orbital launches (38 successes, 1 failure) versus 34 for the United States and 20 for Russia, and the global total hit 114 — the first time more than 100 orbital launches were performed in a single year since 1990, a 25% jump on 2017's 91. The shift is not that the US declined but that a third pole emerged.

raw_evidence.label: BENCHMARK: orbital launch is now highly reliable
raw_evidence.content: For any success/failure analysis, the relevant benchmark is that mature orbital launch is now a high-reliability activity. In this dataset every major launching state sits between roughly 89% and 98% success (e.g. France/Europe ~98%, Russia ~97%, USSR ~95%, China ~96%, US ~92%, India ~89%), and overall 5,384 of 5,726 attempts succeeded (~94%). Externally this is corroborated: the Soyuz/R-7 family exceeds 97% success across 2,000+ flights, and CSIS reports China's Long March at a 95.3% success rate — comparable to the US Delta (95.5%) and Soyuz (97.2%). So the 'new contenders' are not cutting corners on reliability; China and the commercial entrants are competitive with the incumbents on this dimension. Treat sub-90% or early-program failure clusters (e.g. SpaceX's three early Falcon 1 failures) as the exceptions that prove a high baseline, not the norm.

raw_evidence.label: The first commercial wave: Arianespace
raw_evidence.content: Long before SpaceX, the 'private' agency_type in this data was led by Europe. Arianespace, founded on 1980-03-26, was the world's first commercial launch-service provider, created to commercialize the European Space Agency's Ariane rockets. In the dataset, Arianespace (agency code 'AE', state 'F' for France/Europe) accounts for 258 launches — the largest single 'private' provider before the SpaceX era, and its Ariane 5 is among the most-flown vehicles in the data. This matters for interpreting the agency_type field: 'private' is not new — it dates to 1980 and grew steadily through the 1990s-2000s — whereas 'startup' is the genuinely recent category. An analyst tracking 'commercialization' should distinguish the older Arianespace-style commercial providers from the newer venture-backed startups.

raw_evidence.label: Two commercialization waves: Arianespace (1984) then startups (2006)
raw_evidence.content: A new KIND of actor appears late. 'Startup' launches (almost all SpaceX, plus Rocket Lab) first appear in 2006 and reach 8.8% of all launches in the 2010s. The older 'private' commercial category (led by Arianespace from 1984) peaked earlier — 30.9% of launches in the 1990s and 46.9% in the 2000s — then fell to 36.3% in the 2010s as STATE launches rebounded (China). So commercialization is not one monotonic trend: an Arianespace-style commercial wave (1984-2000s) was followed by a venture-startup wave (2006-), even as a parallel new state surge (China) ran alongside. 'Private' and 'startup' are genuinely different vintages of actor.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_08 ===")
TYPES = ["state", "private", "startup"]
at_year = (launches.groupby(["launch_year", "agency_type"]).size()
           .unstack("agency_type").reindex(columns=TYPES).fillna(0).astype(int))
at_year = at_year.reindex(range(yr_min, yr_max + 1), fill_value=0)
first_year = {t: int(launches[launches.agency_type == t].launch_year.min()) for t in TYPES}
print("first appearance year by agency_type:", first_year)
at_dec = (launches.groupby(["decade", "agency_type"]).size()
          .unstack("agency_type").reindex(columns=TYPES).fillna(0).astype(int))
at_dec_share = at_dec.div(at_dec.sum(axis=1), axis=0).mul(100).round(1)
print("agency_type share by decade (%):")
print(at_dec_share.to_string())
derived["ana_08"] = dt(
    "Agency-type share of launches by decade (%): state vs private vs startup",
    ["decade"] + TYPES,
    [[f"{int(d)}s"] + [float(at_dec_share.loc[d, t]) for t in TYPES] for d in at_dec_share.index],
)
derived["ana_08b_year"] = dt(
    "Agency-type launches per year (for stacked-area)",
    ["year"] + TYPES,
    [[int(y)] + [int(at_year.loc[y, t]) for t in TYPES] for y in at_year.index],
)

raw_evidence.label: The smallsat new entrant: Rocket Lab Electron
raw_evidence.content: The other 'startup' in the data is Rocket Lab, whose Electron rocket appears with its first orbital flights. Electron reached orbit on 2018-01-21, deploying three CubeSats, and flew its first commercial mission on 2018-11-11. Electron is a dedicated small-satellite launcher — built to carry 200-300 kg to a Sun-synchronous orbit — and it opened up frequent, dedicated access to orbit for small-satellite operators, a segment previously stuck hitching rides as secondary payloads. Its presence (alongside SpaceX) signals a second axis of the 'new contenders' story that runs orthogonal to the country story: not just new nations, but a new class of small, commercial, high-cadence launch providers emerging right at the dataset's edge.

raw_evidence.label: The 'startup' contender: SpaceX and reusability
raw_evidence.content: The data carries a rare third agency_type beyond 'state' and 'private': 'startup', and in this dataset it is almost entirely SpaceX (62 Falcon 9 + 5 Falcon 1 + 1 Falcon Heavy = 68 rows; Rocket Lab supplies the rest). SpaceX was founded in 2002. After three failures that nearly bankrupted it, Falcon 1 reached orbit on 2008-09-28, the first privately developed, fully liquid-fueled rocket to do so. Falcon 9 first flew on 2010-06-04; in December 2015 SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 first stage back on the ground, the breakthrough toward reusability; and the Falcon Heavy first flew on 2018-02-06 — landing its two side boosters simultaneously — squarely inside this dataset's window. The 'startup' label is the data's way of marking a genuinely new kind of actor: a venture-funded private firm driving launch costs down through reuse, distinct from the older state-contractor 'private' providers.

raw_evidence.label: The first commercial wave: Arianespace
raw_evidence.content: Long before SpaceX, the 'private' agency_type in this data was led by Europe. Arianespace, founded on 1980-03-26, was the world's first commercial launch-service provider, created to commercialize the European Space Agency's Ariane rockets. In the dataset, Arianespace (agency code 'AE', state 'F' for France/Europe) accounts for 258 launches — the largest single 'private' provider before the SpaceX era, and its Ariane 5 is among the most-flown vehicles in the data. This matters for interpreting the agency_type field: 'private' is not new — it dates to 1980 and grew steadily through the 1990s-2000s — whereas 'startup' is the genuinely recent category. An analyst tracking 'commercialization' should distinguish the older Arianespace-style commercial providers from the newer venture-backed startups.

raw_evidence.label: Before SpaceX, commercial meant Europe: Arianespace 260 launches

sentences.context: Why any of this matters beyond a leaderboard: who can launch, and how cheaply, decides who controls the satellites that run modern life — communications, navigation, Earth observation, reconnaissance — and the business around them is projected to grow from about $350 billion in 2016 toward more than $1 trillion by 2040.
sentences.summary: det_14: Why it matters: launch access is national power and a $1tn market. Source: How is China Advancing its Space Launch Capabilities? — CSIS ChinaPower (https://chinapower.csis.org/china-space-launch/) Facts: Space technologies underpin communications, navigation (GPS, GLONASS, BeiDou), Earth observation, and military reconnaissance / early warning; only a handful of nations have indigenous launch capability; The global space economy is projected to grow from about $350 billion (2016) to over $1 trillion by 2040, with reusable rockets reducing launch costs

raw_evidence.label: Why it matters: launch access is national power and a $1tn market
raw_evidence.content: Why a general reader should care: who can launch, and how cheaply, decides who controls the satellites that run modern life — communications, navigation (GPS, GLONASS, BeiDou), Earth observation, and military reconnaissance and early warning. Indigenous launch capability is held by only a handful of nations and is treated as a marker of top-tier technological and strategic power; everyone else depends on those few providers. The economics are large and growing: CSIS cites estimates that the global space economy grows from about $350 billion (2016) toward more than $1 trillion by 2040, with reusable rockets sharply cutting launch costs. Against that backdrop, China executed 207 launches in 2010-2019 — more than in the prior four decades combined — narrowing the gap with the US (which in 2018 still spent about $40.1bn on space and operated ~1,327 satellites, versus China's ~$5.8bn and ~363). The 'new contenders' story is really a story about access to space diffusing from two Cold-War superpowers to many state and commercial hands.

raw_evidence.label: Cumulative ledger: the Cold-War duopoly is still 85% of all launches

raw_evidence.label: Concentration: the superpower duopoly's share fell from ~99% to 54%
raw_evidence.content: The single cleanest measure of 'a duel became a crowd': the two Cold-War superpowers' combined share of global launches falls from 100% (1950s) and ~99% (1960s) to 93.5% (1980s), 81.2% (1990s), 70.5% (2000s) and just 54.5% in the 2010s. A 7-group Herfindahl index drops in step from ~6,600 toward ~2,200. The number of countries launching in a decade rose from 2 to 7. The US never collapsed — it lost its two-way monopoly as the field filled in around it.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_07 ===")
top2 = (dec_country["USA"] + dec_country["USSR/Russia"]) / dec_country.sum(axis=1) * 100
# HHI over the 7 country groups (0-10000)
shares_frac = dec_country.div(dec_country.sum(axis=1), axis=0)
hhi = (shares_frac.pow(2).sum(axis=1) * 10000).round(0)
print("decade | top2(US+USSR/Russia)% | HHI(7-group, /10000) | n_countries_with_launch")
n_active = (dec_country > 0).sum(axis=1)
for d in dec_country.index:
    print(f"  {int(d)}s   {top2[d]:5.1f}%             {int(hhi[d]):5d}                {int(n_active[d])}")
derived["ana_07"] = dt(
    "Launch concentration by decade: Cold-War duopoly share + Herfindahl index",
    ["decade", "top2_US_USSR_Russia_pct", "HHI", "countries_active"],
    [[f"{int(d)}s", round(float(top2[d]), 1), int(hhi[d]), int(n_active[d])] for d in dec_country.index],
)

raw_evidence.label: Concentration: the superpower duopoly's share fell from ~99% to 54%
raw_evidence.content: The single cleanest measure of 'a duel became a crowd': the two Cold-War superpowers' combined share of global launches falls from 100% (1950s) and ~99% (1960s) to 93.5% (1980s), 81.2% (1990s), 70.5% (2000s) and just 54.5% in the 2010s. A 7-group Herfindahl index drops in step from ~6,600 toward ~2,200. The number of countries launching in a decade rose from 2 to 7. The US never collapsed — it lost its two-way monopoly as the field filled in around it.

raw_evidence.label: Cumulative ledger: the Cold-War duopoly is still 85% of all launches

Japan (115, 2.0%), India (65, 1.1%) and all others combined (43, 0.8%) form the tail. The cumulative picture is the OLD world; the per-year picture (ana_03) is the new one.

raw_evidence.label: The source: Jonathan McDowell & the JSR Launch Vehicle Database
raw_evidence.content: The numbers come from Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics who has maintained 'Jonathan's Space Report' (JSR) and an associated set of launch catalogs since the 1980s. The JSR Launch Vehicle Database aims to list every type of space launch vehicle, suborbital and orbital, and his master launch log is widely treated as the most complete public record of orbital launch attempts, with launch times to the second where available. It is a reference-grade, hand-curated catalog rather than an official government dataset — which matters for the analyst because edge cases (a launch's success/failure status, an agency's nationality, an org's start/stop dates) reflect McDowell's adjudication. Provenance note: the dataset README links to the LVDB at http://www.planet4589.org/space/lvdb/index.html, which now returns HTTP 404; McDowell reorganized the site (the catalog now lives under planet4589.org/space/gcat and the master launch log at planet4589.org/space/log/launch.html). The data itself is unaffected — only the README's link rotted.

The JSR Launch Vehicle Database aims to list every type of space launch vehicle, suborbital and orbital, and his master launch log is widely treated as the most complete public record of orbital launch attempts, with launch times to the second where available. It is a reference-grade, hand-curated catalog rather than an official government dataset — which matters for the analyst because edge cases (a launch's success/failure status, an agency's nationality, an org's start/stop dates) reflect McDowell's adjudication. Provenance note: the dataset README links to the LVDB at http://www.planet4589.org/space/lvdb/index.html, which now returns HTTP 404; McDowell reorganized the site (the catalog now lives under planet4589.org/space/gcat and the master launch log at planet4589.org/space/log/launch.html). The data itself is unaffected — only the README's link rotted.

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Economist Graphic Detail article + JSR database
raw_evidence.content: This dataset is the data behind The Economist's Graphic Detail piece 'The space race is dominated by new contenders' (published online 2018-10-18; the dataset folder is dated 2018-10-20). The Economist publishes the data and code behind its Graphic Detail charts in a public GitHub repository. The principal source is Jonathan McDowell's JSR Launch Vehicle Database; the agencies table is credited jointly to McDowell and The Economist. Two CSVs ship with it: launches.csv (one row per orbital launch attempt) and agencies.csv (one row per launch-provider organization/phase). The article's headline IS the thesis the data is meant to support — that the set of actors launching into orbit has broadened beyond the original superpowers.
